nameStory: This fungus gets its name from its appearance on maple leaves - the small black spots look remarkably like drops of tar that have been speckled across the leaf surface. Unlike its cousin Black Tar Spot which forms large solid blotches, Speckled Tar Spot creates numerous tiny raised dots that truly resemble tar splatter from a road construction project.
description: Speckled Tar Spot is a common leaf fungus that creates distinctive small black spots on maple leaves throughout New England. The spots are tiny, raised bumps that feel slightly rough to the touch and appear scattered across the upper leaf surface like pepper flakes. Unlike many leaf diseases that cause yellowing or browning, this fungus creates perfectly black circular spots while leaving the rest of the leaf green and healthy-looking. The spots typically measure just a few millimeters across but can be quite numerous on a single leaf.

idTips.label: Small black raised spots
idTips.description: Look for tiny black circles that stick up slightly from the leaf surface, feeling like small bumps when you run your finger across them

idTips.label: Dense groupings
idTips.description: Spots cluster together in patches, often with dozens of tiny black dots concentrated in one area of the leaf

idTips.label: Upper leaf surface only
idTips.description: Check the top side of leaves - you won't find these spots on the undersides, making identification easier

idTips.label: Maple leaves exclusively
idTips.description: Only appears on maple species - if you're looking at oak, birch, or other trees, this isn't your fungus

idTips.label: Persistent black color
idTips.description: The spots stay jet black even when the rest of the leaf turns yellow or brown in fall, creating a striking contrast

idTips.label: Healthy surrounding tissue
idTips.description: The leaf tissue around each spot remains green and healthy-looking, without yellowing halos or dead zones

habitat: Found throughout New England wherever maple trees grow, from backyard sugar maples to forest red maples and swamp maples in wetland areas. Most commonly spotted in mixed deciduous forests, suburban landscapes, and along woodland edges where maples thrive. The fungus seems equally happy on maples growing in rich forest soils or more marginal urban conditions.

seasonality.spring: Fungal spores begin infecting new maple leaves as they emerge, but visible spots won't appear until later in the growing season.
seasonality.summer: Black spots become increasingly visible from mid to late summer as the fungus matures, appearing as small dark bumps on otherwise healthy green leaves.
seasonality.fall: Peak identification time - the black spots become most obvious as they remain dark against yellowing and reddening maple foliage, creating striking contrast.
seasonality.winter: Spots may still be visible on fallen leaves beneath trees, though most leaves will have decomposed by this point.

funFact: This fungus is actually helping the maple tree by staying put - unlike many leaf diseases that spread throughout the leaf killing large areas, Speckled Tar Spot creates tiny isolated "islands" that barely harm the tree, almost like it has learned to be a polite houseguest that doesn't overstay its welcome.
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with Black Tar Spot, but that forms large solid black patches rather than tiny speckled dots. Remember: speckled means small and scattered like pepper, while black tar spot looks like someone dropped a blob of paint on the leaf.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its somewhat alarming appearance, this fungus rarely causes serious harm to maple trees and is considered more of a cosmetic issue than a health threat. Many people mistake it for insect damage or pollution spots, but the perfectly round raised shape gives away its fungal identity.
compareHints: Speckled Tar Spot creates numerous tiny raised dots, while Black Tar Spot forms larger solid patches that can cover significant portions of a leaf. American Tar Spot tends to create medium-sized spots between these two extremes. The "speckled" pattern of many small dots clustered together is the key distinguishing feature of this species.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Black Tar Spot creates the largest and most solid-looking black spots compared to its relatives.
American Tar Spot creates larger, more irregular black patches compared to Black Tar Spot, which tends to form smaller, more circular spots.
